analyses.question: How has NVIDIA's revenue and growth outlook changed over the last two years?

brief.title: NVIDIA Revenue Trajectory: FY2024–FY2026 YTD Acceleration and Emerging Headwinds
brief.executiveSummary: NVIDIA's revenue has compounded at extraordinary rates over the past two fiscal years, rising from $26,974 million in FY2023 to $60,922 million in FY2024 (up 126%) and then to $130,497 million in FY2025 (up 114%), driven almost entirely by Data Center demand for AI accelerated computing. Into FY2026, year-on-year growth remains strong—up 69% in Q1 and 56% in Q2—but the pace is moderating sequentially and gross margins have compressed from prior-year peaks, partly due to a $4.5 billion H20 export-control charge in Q1 FY2026. The growth outlook remains positive but is increasingly subject to export restrictions, customer concentration, and the complexity of transitioning from Hopper to Blackwell architecture at scale.

keyFindings.title: Revenue more than quadrupled in two fiscal years
keyFindings.finding: Total revenue grew from $26,974 million in FY2023 to $60,922 million in FY2024 (up 126%) and to $130,497 million in FY2025 (up 114%). Data Center revenue was the primary engine, rising from $15,005 million in FY2023 to $47,525 million in FY2024 and $115,186 million in FY2025.

keyFindings.title: FY2026 YTD growth remains strong but is decelerating
keyFindings.finding: Q1 FY2026 revenue was $44,062 million, up 69% year-on-year; Q2 FY2026 revenue was $46,743 million, up 56% year-on-year; Q3 FY2026 revenue was $57,006 million, up 62% year-on-year. Sequential growth has been positive each quarter (12%, 6%, and 22%), indicating continued momentum but at a lower rate than the triple-digit annual growth of FY2024–FY2025.

keyFindings.title: Compute & Networking segment is the dominant growth driver
keyFindings.finding: Compute & Networking segment revenue grew from $15,068 million in FY2023 to $47,405 million in FY2024 (up 215%) and $116,193 million in FY2025 (up 145%). In Q1 FY2026, the segment reached $39,589 million (up 75% year-on-year), and in Q3 FY2026 it continued to lead growth driven by Blackwell architecture demand and NVLink networking.

keyFindings.title: Gross margin expanded through FY2025 but compressed in FY2026
keyFindings.finding: Gross margin improved from 56.9% in FY2023 to 72.7% in FY2024 and 75.0% in FY2025, driven by Data Center revenue mix. In FY2026, gross margin fell to 60.5% in Q1 (impacted by the $4.5 billion H20 charge), recovered to 72.4% in Q2, and reached 73.4% in Q3. Management attributed the year-on-year compression to Blackwell full-scale datacenter systems having a different cost structure than prior Hopper HGX systems.

keyFindings.title: H20 export controls introduced a material one-time revenue and margin risk
keyFindings.finding: On April 9, 2025, the U.S. government required a license for H20 exports to China. NVIDIA incurred a $4.5 billion charge in Q1 FY2026 for H20 excess inventory and purchase obligations. H20 sales were $4.6 billion in Q1 FY2026 prior to the new requirements, and the filing states the requirements 'will also negatively affect our future revenue.' There were no H20 sales to China-based customers in Q2 FY2026.

keyFindings.title: Customer concentration in Compute & Networking has intensified
keyFindings.finding: In FY2024, one direct customer represented 13% of total revenue. By FY2025, three direct customers each exceeded 10% of total revenue (12%, 11%, 11%). In Q3 FY2026, four direct customers exceeded 10% each (22%, 15%, 13%, 11%), all attributable to the Compute & Networking segment. Management noted this concentration trend 'may continue.'

investmentConsiderations.text: Export control risk is now a structural revenue constraint. The H20 licensing requirement imposed in April 2025 resulted in a $4.5 billion charge and eliminated China-bound H20 sales. Management explicitly stated this 'will also negatively affect our future revenue.' Diligence teams should assess the size of the China-addressable market that is now effectively closed and whether alternative geographies or products can offset this loss.

Gross margin trajectory warrants monitoring through the Blackwell transition. Margins peaked at 75.0% in FY2025 and have compressed year-on-year in FY2026 as Blackwell full-scale datacenter systems carry a different cost structure than prior Hopper HGX systems. The Q1 FY2026 H20 charge further distorted the margin profile. Whether Blackwell margins recover to FY2025 levels as the architecture matures is a key variable.

Customer concentration in the Compute & Networking segment has intensified and creates revenue volatility risk. In Q3 FY2026, four customers each exceeded 10% of total revenue (the largest at 22%), all in Compute & Networking. Management acknowledged this trend 'may continue.' A pullback or budget shift by any single hyperscaler could have an outsized impact on quarterly results.

Operating expense growth is accelerating in absolute terms, though declining as a percentage of revenue. R&D expenses rose from $8,675 million in FY2024 to $12,914 million in FY2025 (up 49%), driven by a 234% increase in engineering development costs for new product introductions and a 100% increase in compute and infrastructure. As revenue growth moderates toward the 56–69% year-on-year range seen in FY2026 YTD, operating leverage will depend on whether expense growth can be contained.

brief.title: Cloud Business Comparison: Microsoft Azure, AWS, and Google Cloud
brief.executiveSummary: All three hyperscalers are growing their cloud businesses rapidly, with AI integration serving as the primary demand driver across each platform. Google Cloud is the fastest-growing of the three on a percentage basis (36% revenue growth in FY2025), while AWS remains the most profitable cloud segment in absolute operating income terms among the three. Microsoft's Azure posted 40% growth in the most recent quarter (FY2026Q1) and its broader Microsoft Cloud reached $49.1 billion in that single quarter, reflecting the scale advantage of bundling productivity, infrastructure, and AI services. Meaningful direct comparison is constrained by differing segment definitions and reporting periods across the three companies.

keyFindings.title: Google Cloud Revenue Surged 36% to $58.7 Billion in FY2025
keyFindings.finding: Google Cloud revenues grew from $43,229 million in 2024 to $58,705 million in 2025, a 36% increase. Segment operating income more than doubled, rising from $6,112 million to $13,910 million over the same period, reflecting improving unit economics as the business scales.

keyFindings.title: Microsoft Cloud Quarterly Revenue Hit $49.1 Billion, Azure Up 40%
keyFindings.finding: In FY2026Q1 (quarter ended September 30, 2025), Microsoft Cloud revenue increased 26% to $49.1 billion. Azure and other cloud services revenue grew 40% in that quarter. The commercial remaining performance obligation — a forward-looking indicator of contracted future revenue — increased 51% to $392 billion.

keyFindings.title: AWS Is Amazon's Dedicated Cloud Segment; Financials Not Fully Excerpted
keyFindings.finding: Amazon organizes its operations into three segments: North America, International, and AWS. AWS serves developers and enterprises with compute, storage, database, analytics, AI/ML, and other on-demand technology services. Detailed AWS revenue and operating income figures for FY2025 are referenced in the filing but the specific financial table was not included in the provided excerpts.

keyFindings.title: Google Cloud Profitability Has Improved Sharply Over Three Years
keyFindings.finding: Google Cloud operating income grew from $1,716 million in 2023 to $6,112 million in 2024 to $13,910 million in 2025, demonstrating a rapid trajectory toward higher margins. Total Google Cloud costs and expenses rose from $31,372 million in 2023 to $44,795 million in 2025, with employee compensation and other costs both increasing, but revenue growth has outpaced cost growth.

keyFindings.title: AI Is the Core Growth Driver Across All Three Cloud Platforms
keyFindings.finding: All three companies cite AI as the primary demand catalyst for their cloud businesses. Microsoft highlights Azure AI consumption-based services and its OpenAI partnership; Google Cloud emphasizes its full-stack AI approach including custom TPUs (Ironwood), Gemini Enterprise, and AI-powered cybersecurity; AWS is described as offering broad AI/ML services to enterprises. Each company is making significant capital investments in infrastructure to meet AI-driven demand.

keyFindings.title: Microsoft Cloud Bundles Productivity and Infrastructure; Broadest Definition
keyFindings.finding: Microsoft's 'Microsoft Cloud' metric aggregates Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud, Azure and other cloud services, the commercial portion of LinkedIn, and Dynamics 365 — a broader definition than a pure infrastructure cloud. Azure specifically covers cloud and AI consumption-based services, GitHub cloud, Nuance Healthcare cloud, virtual desktop, and other cloud services. This bundled approach differentiates Microsoft's go-to-market from AWS and Google Cloud, which are more narrowly defined enterprise cloud platforms.

investmentConsiderations.text: Google Cloud's operating income trajectory — from $1,716 million in 2023 to $13,910 million in 2025 — suggests a business that is still in a margin expansion phase. A diligence team should assess whether this improvement is structural (scale leverage, pricing power) or partly cyclical, and how the pending $32.0 billion Wiz acquisition (expected to close in 2026) will affect cloud segment margins and competitive positioning in cybersecurity.

Microsoft's $392 billion commercial remaining performance obligation (up 51% year-over-year) provides exceptional forward revenue visibility, but also reflects long-duration contractual commitments that require sustained delivery on AI and cloud roadmaps. The bundled nature of 'Microsoft Cloud' (Azure + M365 + Dynamics + LinkedIn) makes it difficult to isolate pure infrastructure cloud economics, which is a key consideration when benchmarking against AWS or Google Cloud.

All three companies are making significant and increasing capital expenditures in AI infrastructure (datacenters, GPUs, custom chips). Alphabet reported capital expenditures of $91.4 billion for FY2025, primarily for technical infrastructure. Microsoft explicitly notes that cloud and AI infrastructure investments will continue to increase operating costs and may decrease operating margins. Diligence teams should model the capex intensity trajectory and its impact on free cash flow conversion for each platform.

Regulatory and compliance risk is explicitly flagged for Google Cloud, particularly for financial services, healthcare, and public sector customers, including exposure to government audits, sovereign operating requirements, and evolving data localization laws. Microsoft similarly highlights security and compliance as a competitive differentiator, suggesting these are both risks and potential moats depending on execution.

Economic Conditions, Challenges, and RisksThe markets for software, devices, and cloud-based services are dynamic and highly competitive. The devices and form factors customers prefer evolve rapidly, influencing how users access services in the cloud and, in some cases, the user’s choice of which suite of cloud-based services to use. We must continue to evolve and adapt over an extended time in pace with this changing environment.The investments we are making in cloud and AI infrastructure and devices will continue to increase our operating costs and may decrease our operating margins. We continue to identify and evaluate opportunities to expand our datacenter locations and increase our server capacity to meet the evolving needs of our customers, particularly given the growing demand for AI services. Our devices are primarily manufactured by third-party contract manufacturers. ITEM 1.BUSINESSOverviewAs our founders Larry and Sergey wrote in the original founders' letter, "Google is not a conventional company. We do not intend to become one." That unconventional spirit has been a driving force throughout our history, inspiring us to tackle big problems and invest in moonshots. It led us to be a pioneer in the development of artificial intelligence (AI) and, since 2016, be an AI-first company. We continue this work under the leadership of Alphabet and Google CEO, Sundar Pichai.Alphabet is a collection of businesses — the largest of which is Google. We report Google in two segments, Google Services and Google Cloud, and all non-Google businesses collectively as Other Bets. Supporting these businesses, we have centralized certain AI-related research and development focused on advanced research in AI and developing the frontier models that serve our businesses, which is reported in Alphabet-level activities. Alphabet's structure is about helping each of our businesses prosper through strong leaders and independence.Access and Technology for EveryoneThe Internet is one of the world’s most powerful equalizers; it propels ideas, people, and businesses large and small. Our mission to organize the world’s information and make it universally accessible and useful is as relevant today as it was when we were founded in 1998. Since then, we have evolved from a company that helps people find answers to a company that also helps people get things done. We are focused on building an even more helpful Google for everyone, and we aspire to give everyone the tools they need to increase their knowledge, health, happiness, and success. Google Search helps people find information and make sense of the world in more natural and intuitive ways, with trillions of searches on Google every year. YouTube provides people with entertainment, information, and opportunities to learn something new and helps support the creator economy through the YouTube Partner Program. Google Cloud helps customers build for the future, improve productivity, reduce costs, and unlock new growth engines. We continually innovate and build new products and features to help our users, partners, customers, and communities and have invested more than $200 billion in research and development in the last five years in support of these efforts.3.

brief.title: Apple Regulatory Disclosure Evolution: FY2023–FY2025
brief.executiveSummary: Apple's regulatory risk disclosures have grown materially more specific and consequential from FY2023 through FY2025, progressing from forward-looking warnings about the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) compliance deadline to detailed accounts of implemented changes, active Commission challenges, U.S. court orders, and the Google antitrust ruling's direct impact on Apple's search licensing revenue. Management describes a pattern of reactive business changes—to App Store terms, distribution, payment processing, and developer communications—driven by litigation, government investigations, and new legislation across multiple jurisdictions. By FY2025, disclosures also added a new tariff risk section and explicitly acknowledged a U.S. court order prohibiting Apple from collecting commissions on certain purchases, representing a concrete operational constraint absent from earlier filings.

keyFindings.title: DMA Compliance: From Deadline Warning to Active Implementation
keyFindings.finding: In FY2023, Apple disclosed it was required to comply with the EU Digital Markets Act by March 2024 and described future changes as hypothetical. By FY2024, the filing reported that Apple had already implemented changes to iOS, iPadOS, the App Store, and Safari in the EU—including new business terms, alternative fee structures, alternative distribution methods, alternative payment processing, and additional developer APIs—and that its compliance plan had been challenged by the European Commission. FY2025 retained all of this language and added that the DMA provides for significant fines and penalties for noncompliance, and that many privacy and security risks will remain even after Apple's changes.

keyFindings.title: U.S. Court Order on App Store Commissions Appears in FY2025
keyFindings.finding: FY2025 introduced a materially new disclosure absent from FY2023 and FY2024: Apple is currently subject to a court order preventing it from imposing any commission or fee on certain purchases that consumers make through the U.S. storefront of the iOS and iPadOS App Store. This represents a concrete, legally binding operational constraint, not merely a hypothetical risk.

keyFindings.title: Google Antitrust Ruling Adds Direct Revenue Risk in FY2025
keyFindings.finding: FY2023 and FY2024 disclosed that Apple's search licensing arrangements with Google and others were subject to government investigations and legal proceedings. FY2025 added a specific new disclosure: on August 5, 2024, Google was found to have violated U.S. antitrust laws, and on September 2, 2025, the D.C. District Court ordered certain remedies. The filing warns that if DOJ-proposed remedies—such as prohibiting Google from offering Apple commercial terms for search distribution—were implemented, they could materially adversely affect Apple's ability to earn revenue from such licensing arrangements.

keyFindings.title: U.S. Antitrust Lawsuits Explicitly Named Starting FY2024
keyFindings.finding: FY2023 referenced antitrust investigations in various jurisdictions and App Store-related investigations in Europe, but did not name specific U.S. lawsuits. FY2024 and FY2025 both explicitly disclosed that Apple is subject to civil antitrust lawsuits in the U.S. alleging monopolization or attempted monopolization in the markets for 'performance smartphones' and 'smartphones' generally in violation of U.S. antitrust laws.

keyFindings.title: AI/ML Regulatory Risk Added as a New Dimension in FY2024–FY2025
keyFindings.finding: FY2023 disclosures did not reference artificial intelligence or machine learning as a regulatory risk factor. FY2024 added language noting that risks and costs may increase as Apple expands the use of machine learning and artificial intelligence features and must navigate new legal, regulatory and ethical considerations. FY2025 further expanded this, noting that AI integration may exacerbate risks of novel IP claims and that AI features can increase risks of inadvertent personal data disclosure.

keyFindings.title: FY2025 Adds New Tariff Risk Section Absent from Prior Years
keyFindings.finding: FY2025 introduced a dedicated 'Tariffs and Other Measures' section in the MD&A, disclosing that beginning in the second quarter of 2025, new U.S. tariffs were announced on imports from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam, and the EU, among others, and that several countries have imposed or threatened reciprocal tariffs. The filing notes that a U.S. Department of Commerce investigation under Section 232 has been initiated into semiconductor imports and their derivative products. This risk category was not present in FY2023 or FY2024 filings.

investmentConsiderations.text: The progression from hypothetical DMA risk (FY2023) to implemented changes under active Commission challenge (FY2024–FY2025) indicates that regulatory compliance is no longer a future contingency but an ongoing operational reality with iterative cost and business model implications. The DMA's significant fines and penalties for noncompliance remain a live exposure.

The FY2025 disclosure of a U.S. court order prohibiting Apple from collecting commissions or fees on certain App Store purchases, combined with the Google antitrust remedies that could bar commercial search distribution terms, represents a concentration of concrete revenue risks to the Services segment that were not present in FY2023 disclosures. Diligence teams should assess the financial materiality of these specific constraints.

The new FY2025 tariff section—covering imports from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam, and the EU, plus a Section 232 semiconductor investigation—introduces supply chain and cost structure risks that are distinct from the legal/regulatory risks dominating prior years' disclosures. The filing notes the ultimate impact remains uncertain.

The expanding AI/ML regulatory risk language across FY2024 and FY2025 suggests that as Apple Intelligence and related features are deployed, the company anticipates incremental legal, regulatory, and data privacy exposure. Management acknowledges that AI features can increase risks of inadvertent personal data disclosure, which could trigger additional compliance obligations.
